can-you-drink-the-tap-water-in-tenerife.question: Can you drink the tap water in Tenerife?
can-you-drink-the-tap-water-in-tenerife.title: Can You Drink the Tap Water in Tenerife?
can-you-drink-the-tap-water-in-tenerife.meta: Tenerife's tap water is treated to EU drinking standards and is safe, but most residents and visitors drink bottled water because of the taste. Here is why.
can-you-drink-the-tap-water-in-tenerife.short: Yes. Tap water in Tenerife is treated to EU drinking-water standards and is safe to drink. Most residents and visitors still buy bottled water, because the taste — a legacy of desalination and the island's volcanic geology — puts a lot of people off. It is a preference, not a health warning.

sections.h2: Safe, but not to everyone's taste
p: Spain applies EU drinking-water rules, and Tenerife's supply is treated and monitored to meet them. Brushing your teeth, filling a glass, cooking with it and making coffee are all completely normal here, and nobody boils water before use.

What people object to is flavour. Much of the island's water is either desalinated seawater or comes up through volcanic rock via galerías, the tunnels bored horizontally into the mountains to reach groundwater. Both routes leave mineral characteristics that many describe as flat, faintly salty or slightly metallic. Coffee made with it tastes different from what you are used to.

You will see signs in some hotel bathrooms advising guests not to drink from the tap. This is usually caution rather than a statement about the municipal supply: hotels cannot vouch for their own internal plumbing, storage tanks and pipework, and a blanket sign is simpler than explaining the distinction.
Water quality also varies by municipality, since supply and treatment are handled locally rather than island-wide. Water in one town can taste noticeably different from water twenty minutes away.

The follow-up question is usually about everything made with water rather than the water itself. Ice in bars and restaurants, salad washed in the kitchen, coffee, and juice made up from concentrate are all fine, because they all start from the same supply that meets the same standards.

This is worth saying plainly because travellers arriving from countries where tap water genuinely is a risk often carry the habits with them — refusing ice, avoiding salad. None of that is necessary in Tenerife, and it will make eating out unnecessarily awkward.

Buy the large five- or eight-litre bottles from a supermarket rather than small ones from a beach kiosk. The price difference is substantial and it cuts the plastic considerably. A refillable bottle plus one big supermarket bottle covers a family for days.

If you would rather not buy water at all, a filter jug or filter bottle deals with the taste without dealing with a health problem, because there was not one to begin with. Restaurants will bring bottled water by default; if you want tap, ask for agua del grifo, and be aware that some places will politely tell you they only serve bottled.
list: Safe to drink and to cook with
Taste is the objection, not safety
Large supermarket bottles are far cheaper
Ask for agua del grifo if you want tap

faq: Can you brush your teeth with tap water in Tenerife?
Yes, without any concern. The water meets EU drinking-water standards.
Why does Tenerife tap water taste salty?
Much of the supply is desalinated seawater or groundwater drawn through volcanic rock, and both leave a mineral character that many people find flat or faintly salty.
Is bottled water expensive in Tenerife?
Not from supermarkets, where large bottles cost very little. Small bottles from beach kiosks and hotel minibars cost many times more.

is-tenerife-expensive.question: Is Tenerife expensive?
is-tenerife-expensive.title: Is Tenerife Expensive? What Things Actually Cost
is-tenerife-expensive.meta: Tenerife is one of the cheaper warm-winter destinations in Europe, but costs vary hugely between the resorts. Where the money goes and how to cut the bill.
is-tenerife-expensive.alt: Produce stalls at the Mercado de Nuestra Señora de África in Santa Cruz
is-tenerife-expensive.short: By European standards, no. The Canaries have lower sales tax than mainland Spain, and eating and drinking away from the seafront is inexpensive. But the gap between resorts is large: the same day costs far more in Costa Adeje than in Los Cristianos or the north, and almost all of the difference is under your control.

p: The Canary Islands do not use mainland Spain's VAT. They apply their own lower indirect tax, which is one reason alcohol, tobacco, fuel and electronics are noticeably cheaper here than on the mainland or in northern Europe.

Public transport is the other bargain. TITSA buses cover the island for a few euros a journey, and the tram between Santa Cruz and La Laguna costs well under two euros. Beaches are free, most viewpoints are free, and the walking — Anaga, the Teide crater floor, the coastal promenades — costs nothing at all.

Seafront restaurants in Costa Adeje and Playa de las Américas charge resort prices, and the mark-up over a place one street back is often startling for identical food. Sunbed and parasol hire at the smartest beaches runs to the higher end of ten to fifteen euros a day, while quieter beaches charge noticeably less and many people just bring a towel.

Attractions are the real budget item. Siam Park costs from around forty euros for an adult day ticket, with a twin ticket combining it with Loro Parque at roughly seventy. Whale-watching trips start from about thirty euros. Two attraction days for a family adds up faster than a week of meals.
rows: Booking online is normally cheaper than at the gate
Only worth it if you will use both; they are 90 min apart
Two to three hours, smaller boats cost more
Sunbed and parasol, Playa del Duque
Less at Los Cristianos and the quieter beaches
Bus, Los Cristianos to Costa Adeje
TITSA; the tram in Santa Cruz is under €2

sections.h2: The four things that move your budget most
p: Choosing the resort does most of the work. Costa Adeje is the island's most expensive base and Los Cristianos, twenty minutes south, is meaningfully cheaper for the same sunshine. The north — Puerto de la Cruz and around — is cheaper again, at the cost of cooler and cloudier weather.

After that it is habits rather than luck. Eat where the menu is not translated into five languages. Look for the menú del día at lunch, which is the cheapest proper meal of the day almost anywhere in Spain. Buy water and breakfast things from a supermarket rather than a kiosk. And be honest about whether you need a hire car, because if you are staying put in the south you probably do not.
list: Pick the resort deliberately — it is the biggest lever
Eat one street back from the seafront
Menú del día at lunch, not dinner
Skip the car if you are not leaving the resort

faq: Is Tenerife cheaper than mainland Spain?

For alcohol, tobacco, fuel and electronics, yes, because the Canaries apply their own lower indirect tax rather than mainland VAT. Restaurant and hotel prices in the big resorts are comparable to or above the mainland.
What is a menú del día?
A fixed-price lunch — usually a starter, a main, dessert or coffee, and a drink. It is the cheapest way to eat a proper meal in Spain and is served at lunchtime on weekdays.
Which part of Tenerife is cheapest?
The north, around Puerto de la Cruz, and in the south Los Cristianos rather than Costa Adeje. Costa Adeje is the most expensive base on the island.

what-is-calima-in-tenerife.question: What is calima in Tenerife?
what-is-calima-in-tenerife.title: What Is Calima in Tenerife? Saharan Dust Explained
what-is-calima-in-tenerife.meta: Calima is Saharan dust carried over the Canaries on an easterly wind. What it does to the weather, when it happens and what it means for your holiday.
what-is-calima-in-tenerife.alt: A Canary Islands city under thick orange Saharan calima
what-is-calima-in-tenerife.short: Calima is a haze of fine dust and sand blown over the Canary Islands from the Sahara on an easterly wind. It turns the sky yellow-orange, pushes temperatures up sharply and cuts visibility. Most episodes are mild and pass in a day or two; severe ones are rare but can disrupt flights.

p: Tenerife sits around three hundred kilometres off the coast of Africa. When the wind swings round to the east, it carries suspended dust from the Sahara out over the islands. The word calima simply describes that haze.

The visible effect is a milky or orange sky, a sun you can look at, and horizons that vanish — on a strong calima day you cannot see La Gomera from the south coast, and Teide disappears from the motorway. Temperatures often jump several degrees at the same time, because the air arriving is desert air.

sections.h2: When it happens, and how bad it gets
p: Calima is most common between late autumn and early spring, though it can occur in any month. Most episodes are mild: a hazy day or two, warmer than forecast, and then the trade winds resume and clear it out.

Severe events are much rarer. In February 2020 an exceptionally heavy calima cut visibility so badly that flights across the Canaries were suspended and both Tenerife airports closed for a period. That was unusual enough to make international news, which is precisely why it is worth knowing it is not the norm.

sections.h2: What it means for your trip
p: For most visitors, a mild calima means a hot hazy day and disappointing photographs. Anyone with asthma or another respiratory condition should take it more seriously: fine airborne dust aggravates those conditions, and the sensible response is to stay indoors with the windows shut on the worst days and keep any inhaler to hand.

It also means the Teide cable car view can be worthless on a calima day, since you may be looking down at haze rather than out at the islands. If you have the flexibility, that is a trip worth moving. Check the Spanish met office, AEMET, which forecasts calima episodes, and if you are flying during a heavy one, check your flight status before travelling to the airport.
list: Hazy skies and a sharp jump in temperature
Most common late autumn to early spring
Respiratory conditions need real care
Worth postponing a Teide trip

faq: How long does calima last in Tenerife?
Most episodes last a day or two before the trade winds clear the air. Longer spells happen but are less common.
Is calima dangerous?
For most people it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. People with asthma or other respiratory conditions should limit time outdoors during heavy episodes.
Does calima cancel flights?
Rarely. It takes an exceptionally heavy episode to reduce visibility enough to stop flights, as happened across the Canaries in February 2020. Mild calima has no effect on air travel.
Can you still swim during calima?
Yes. Calima affects the air, not the water. The main change is that it is usually hotter and the light is poor.

tenerife-or-gran-canaria.question: Tenerife or Gran Canaria — which should you choose?
tenerife-or-gran-canaria.title: Tenerife or Gran Canaria? An Honest Comparison
tenerife-or-gran-canaria.meta: Tenerife and Gran Canaria offer similar winter sun but suit different trips. Landscape, resorts, nightlife, beaches and getting around, compared honestly.
tenerife-or-gran-canaria.alt: The dunes at Maspalomas on Gran Canaria
tenerife-or-gran-canaria.short: Both deliver reliable winter sun and cost about the same. Choose Tenerife if you want dramatic landscape, Spain's highest mountain and more variety in a single trip. Choose Gran Canaria if you want the famous Maspalomas dunes, a genuinely walkable city beach at Las Palmas, and everything packed into a smaller area.

p: Tenerife is the larger island and by some distance the more dramatic. Teide rises to 3,715 metres, the Anaga range in the north-east holds an ancient laurel forest, and the Los Gigantes cliffs fall five hundred metres straight into the sea. You can be on a beach in the morning and above the clouds by lunchtime, and the north and south feel like different countries.

Gran Canaria is often described as a continent in miniature, and it earns it — but on a smaller canvas. Its signature landscape is the Maspalomas dunes in the south, a genuine desert of sand beside the sea, which Tenerife has nothing to match.

Gran Canaria concentrates its tourism in the south around Maspalomas and Playa del Inglés, which between them hold huge beaches and the best-established LGBT+ scene in the archipelago. Las Palmas in the north is the real difference-maker: a full-sized city with Playa de las Canteras, a long urban beach good enough to swim at daily, which no Tenerife city offers.

Tenerife spreads its resorts along the south-west coast, from the upmarket Costa Adeje through the busy Playa de las Américas to quieter Los Cristianos, with the older, more Canarian Puerto de la Cruz in the north. Its beaches are a mix of imported golden sand in the south and natural black volcanic sand elsewhere.

For a first visit to the Canaries with a hire car and an appetite for scenery, Tenerife gives you more to see and the single most impressive thing in the archipelago in Teide. For a holiday centred on one very good beach with less driving, Gran Canaria is the easier proposition.

Weather is close enough not to decide it. Both have the same pattern: sunnier and drier in the south, cooler and greener in the north. Both are reachable on the same flights and cost broadly the same. There is also a ferry between them, so a trip taking in both is entirely practical if you have two weeks.
list: Tenerife: Teide, Anaga, Los Gigantes, more variety
Gran Canaria: Maspalomas dunes, Las Palmas city beach
Weather and cost are close to identical
Ferries link the two if you want both

faq: Is Tenerife or Gran Canaria better for families?

Both work well. Tenerife has Siam Park and Loro Parque, two of the strongest attractions in the islands. Gran Canaria has larger, calmer southern beaches concentrated in a smaller area, which means less driving.
Which island has better weather?
They are very similar. On both, the south is sunnier and drier and the north is cooler and cloudier. Neither has a meaningful advantage.
Can you visit both on one trip?
Yes. Ferries run between the islands, and it is a realistic plan if you have two weeks. For one week, pick one.

are-there-sharks-in-tenerife.question: Are there sharks in Tenerife?
are-there-sharks-in-tenerife.title: Are There Sharks in Tenerife? Sea Safety
are-there-sharks-in-tenerife.meta: Yes, there are sharks in Canary waters — including the rare angelshark — but attacks are essentially unheard of. The real sea risks in Tenerife are different.
are-there-sharks-in-tenerife.alt: An angelshark camouflaged on the seabed
are-there-sharks-in-tenerife.short: Yes, but not the kind you are worried about. Canary waters hold several shark species, most notably the harmless seabed-dwelling angelshark. Attacks are essentially unheard of. The genuine sea risks here are currents, swell and the occasional Portuguese man o' war.

p: The Canary Islands sit in the open Atlantic, so sharks pass through — that is true of every ocean coastline on Earth. The species most associated with these islands is the angelshark, Squatina squatina, which looks more like a ray than a shark and spends its life half-buried on sandy bottoms. It is critically endangered across most of its former range, and Canary waters are one of its last strongholds, which makes divers here rather pleased to see one.

Large predatory sharks exist in the wider Atlantic but stay in deep water well away from the resort beaches. Attacks on swimmers in the Canaries are so rare that they are not a factor any visitor needs to plan around.

sections.h2: What you should actually be careful of
p: The Atlantic itself is the risk, and it is a real one. Beaches on the north and west coasts face open ocean with strong currents and heavy swell, and several — Benijo and the Anaga beaches in particular — have no lifeguard cover. The flag system is not decorative: red means do not enter, and people drown here every year ignoring it.

The second genuine hazard is the Portuguese man o' war, known locally as the carabela portuguesa. These drift in on certain wind conditions, sometimes in numbers, and their sting is severe. When they arrive, beaches fly the appropriate warning and close. Do not touch them on the sand either, since detached tentacles still sting.
list: Follow the beach flags without exception
North and west beaches have strong currents
Portuguese man o' war stings are serious
Sheltered southern beaches are the safest swimming

sections.h2: If you actually want to see marine life
p: The waters off the south-west coast hold resident pilot whales and bottlenose dolphins year-round, which is unusual and is why whale-watching trips from Los Cristianos, Puerto Colón and Los Gigantes have such a high success rate. Trips run from around thirty euros.

For anything smaller, snorkelling and diving are best on the sheltered south and west coasts. Divers hoping for an angelshark encounter usually go in winter, when the animals come into shallower sandy bays.

faq: Has there ever been a shark attack in Tenerife?
Attacks are essentially unheard of in the Canary Islands. Sharks are present in Atlantic waters, but incidents involving swimmers are not something visitors need to plan around.
What is an angelshark?
A flat, bottom-dwelling shark that resembles a ray. It is critically endangered globally, and Canary waters are one of its last strongholds. It is harmless to swimmers.
Are there jellyfish in Tenerife?
Sometimes, and the Portuguese man o' war — not a true jellyfish — is the one that matters. Their arrival depends on wind and currents, and beaches fly warnings and close when they appear.
Is it safe to swim in the sea in Tenerife?
On the sheltered southern beaches, generally yes. On the exposed north and west coasts, conditions can be dangerous and lifeguard cover is patchy. Always follow the flags.

stargazing-in-tenerife.question: Where can you see the stars in Tenerife?
stargazing-in-tenerife.title: Stargazing in Tenerife: Where and When to Go
stargazing-in-tenerife.meta: Tenerife has some of the clearest night skies in the world, protected by law. Where to go, when to go, and whether to book a tour or drive up yourself.
stargazing-in-tenerife.alt: The Teide Observatory silhouetted under the Milky Way
stargazing-in-tenerife.short: Teide National Park, and it is genuinely world class. High altitude, dry air and a national law limiting light pollution give Tenerife some of the clearest skies on Earth — good enough that professional observatories are sited here. You can drive up yourself for free, or join a guided tour with telescopes.

sections.h2: Why the skies here are so good
p: Three things combine. The park sits above two thousand metres, which puts you above the layer of cloud that the trade winds pile against the mountains — the sea of cloud you look down on from the road. The air above it is unusually dry and stable. And since 1988 Spanish law has restricted lighting and air traffic around the observatories to protect the sky itself.

That is not a tourist claim. The Teide Observatory at Izaña is a working professional facility used by institutions from several countries, and the island is designated a Starlight Reserve. On a moonless night at altitude the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a sense of depth you will not have seen from anywhere in northern Europe.

It costs nothing. Drive up the TF-21 from Vilaflor or La Orotava, or the TF-38, and stop at one of the miradors on the crater floor. The Roques de García car park and the Llano de Ucanca are popular. Bring far more clothing than feels reasonable: at that altitude it drops below freezing at night, and the wind makes it worse.

Two cautions. The mountain roads are winding and unlit, and driving them tired after a long night is where the risk actually lies — not in the stargazing. And avoid the few nights either side of a full moon, which washes out everything faint. Check the moon phase before you commit to a date.

Guided trips leave from the southern resorts most evenings and typically include transport, telescopes, a guide who can actually find things, and often dinner. Sunset-and-stars combinations, which take you up for the sunset above the clouds and stay for the dark, are the most popular format.

The case for a tour is straightforward: someone else drives the mountain road in the dark, the telescopes are better than anything you brought, and you get told what you are looking at. The case for going alone is that it is free and you can stay as long as you like. Both are good nights.
Note that the cable car does not operate at night, so evening trips are about the crater floor rather than the summit.
list: Free to drive up and look
Dress for below freezing, whatever the coast is doing
Avoid the nights around a full moon
Tours handle the driving and bring telescopes

faq: Do you need a telescope to see the Milky Way in Tenerife?
No. On a clear moonless night at altitude in Teide National Park the Milky Way is easily visible to the naked eye. A telescope adds planets and deep-sky objects.
Can you visit the Teide Observatory?

It is a working professional facility, not a public attraction, though guided daytime visits are offered at certain times. Check the observatory's own site for current arrangements before planning around it.
Is stargazing in Tenerife cold?
Yes, genuinely. The crater floor sits above two thousand metres and drops below freezing at night even when the coast is warm. Bring proper layers, hat and gloves.
What is the best time of year for stargazing in Tenerife?
Any month can be excellent, since it depends on the night. Pick a date away from the full moon and check the forecast for calima, which hazes the sky.

is-tenerife-safe.question: Is Tenerife safe?
is-tenerife-safe.title: Is Tenerife Safe? An Honest Look at the Risks
is-tenerife-safe.meta: Tenerife is a very safe destination and violent crime is rare. The real risks are the Atlantic, the mountain roads and the sun — not the streets.
is-tenerife-safe.alt: The palm-lined promenade at Playa del Camisón
is-tenerife-safe.short: Yes. Tenerife is part of Spain and is a very safe place to travel, with violent crime rare and resorts heavily policed. The genuine risks are not criminal: the Atlantic, the mountain roads and the sun account for far more visitor trouble than anything else.

sections.h2: The sea is the real risk
p: If one thing on this page matters, it is this. Tenerife's beaches range from sheltered southern bays where children paddle safely to open Atlantic coastline with heavy swell, powerful currents and no lifeguard on duty. People get into difficulty here every year, and it is almost always at the second kind of beach.

Treat the flag system as an instruction rather than a suggestion. Green means normal conditions, yellow means care, red means do not enter — and red means it whether or not other people are in the water. On the north and west coasts, and at the Anaga beaches in particular, assume there is no lifeguard unless you can see one. If you want reliable swimming, the sheltered southern beaches are genuinely safe.

sections.h2: Driving, and the roads that catch people out
p: The motorways are modern and easy. The mountain roads are a different proposition: the TF-436 to Masca, the Anaga roads and the climbs to Teide are narrow, relentlessly winding and often have a drop on one side and a coach coming the other way. They are not dangerous if you are unhurried and sober, but they punish over-confidence.

Two practical points. Hire-car break-ins at remote trailhead car parks happen often enough to be worth planning around — leave nothing visible, ever. And driving those roads tired after a late night is where the actual risk sits, not in the driving itself.

sections.h2: Crime, and the one thing that annoys people
p: Petty theft is the realistic concern: pickpocketing in crowded resort areas, bags lifted from beaches, things taken from cars. Standard precautions cover it. Violent crime against visitors is rare, and walking back to your hotel at night in the southern resorts is not something to worry about.

The thing that genuinely irritates people is not crime at all: timeshare and holiday-club touts working the busy stretches of Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos, usually opening with a scratch card or a survey. A firm no and continuing to walk ends it. Do not accept a lift to a presentation, however good the prize sounds.
list: Emergency number is 112, as everywhere in the EU
Follow the beach flags without exception
Leave nothing visible in a parked car
Walk past the scratch-card touts

faq: Is Tenerife safe at night?

Yes, in normal terms. The resort areas are busy and policed. Ordinary city sense applies, and the busiest nightlife strip in Playa de las Américas gets rowdy late, which is worth knowing when choosing a hotel.
Is it safe to swim in Tenerife?
On the sheltered southern beaches, yes. On the open north and west coasts, conditions can be genuinely dangerous and lifeguard cover is patchy. Always follow the flags.
What is the emergency number in Tenerife?
112, the same across the EU. It covers police, ambulance and fire and has English-speaking operators.
Are the timeshare touts a scam?
The scratch-card approach is a sales tactic, not a robbery. It costs you a long high-pressure presentation rather than your wallet. Decline and keep walking.

what-language-do-they-speak-in-tenerife.question: What language do they speak in Tenerife?
what-language-do-they-speak-in-tenerife.title: What Language Do They Speak in Tenerife?
what-language-do-they-speak-in-tenerife.meta: Spanish, in a distinctive Canarian accent closer to Latin America than to Madrid. English is widely spoken in the resorts and much less so inland.
what-language-do-they-speak-in-tenerife.alt: A colonial street in La Laguna
what-language-do-they-speak-in-tenerife.short: Spanish. Canarian Spanish has its own accent and vocabulary and sounds closer to Latin America than to mainland Spain. English is widely spoken across the southern resorts, patchily in the north, and barely at all in the small inland villages.

sections.h2: Canarian Spanish is its own thing
p: The official language is Spanish, but if you learned yours in Madrid or from a textbook, the Canarian version will take a moment. Islanders use seseo, pronouncing c and z as s, so cerveza comes out closer to servesa. Final s tends to be aspirated or dropped, which is why las casas can sound like lah casah.

Grammar differs too. Canarians use ustedes where mainland Spain uses vosotros for you plural, exactly as Latin America does. That is not a coincidence: centuries of traffic between the islands and the Americas ran in both directions, and the language went with it.

A handful of everyday Canarian words are not the mainland ones, and knowing four or five of them makes ordering considerably easier. A bus is a guagua, not an autobús. Potatoes are papas, not patatas — which is how you get papas arrugadas, the wrinkled salt-boiled potatoes served with almost everything.

You will also meet millo for maize rather than maíz, and a friendly mi niño or mi niña used to address adults of any age, which is affectionate rather than condescending. Several of these came from Portuguese, another legacy of who was sailing past.
list: guagua — bus
papas — potatoes
millo — maize
mi niño / mi niña — affectionate address
ustedes — you plural, as in Latin America

p: In Costa Adeje, Playa de las Américas and Los Cristianos, comfortably. Menus are translated, hotel staff are fluent, and many businesses are run by long-settled British, German and Italian residents. You can holiday there for a week without a word of Spanish and nobody will blink.

Away from that strip it thins out quickly. In Santa Cruz and La Laguna you will find English in the tourist-facing places and less elsewhere. In the villages of Anaga, Teno and the inland north, assume none. A few words of Spanish are not just useful there — they are noticed and appreciated, because visitors so rarely bother.
One thing that is often confused: the whistled language, silbo, belongs to La Gomera, the island you can see from the south coast. It is not spoken in Tenerife.

faq: Do I need to speak Spanish in Tenerife?
Not in the southern resorts, where English is spoken everywhere. Away from them it helps a great deal, and in the inland villages it is close to essential.
Is Canarian Spanish hard to understand?

It is a distinct accent — s sounds are softened or dropped and the rhythm is faster — but it is standard Spanish underneath. Learners who know Latin American Spanish usually find it easier than mainland Spanish.
What is the whistled language of the Canary Islands?
Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish used to communicate across the ravines of La Gomera. It is recognised by UNESCO and taught in schools there, but it belongs to La Gomera, not Tenerife.
Is Guanche still spoken?
No. The language of the island's pre-conquest inhabitants died out, though it survives in place names such as Taganana and Anaga and in a few everyday words.

can-you-swim-in-the-sea-in-tenerife-in-w.question: Can you swim in the sea in Tenerife in winter?
can-you-swim-in-the-sea-in-tenerife-in-w.title: Can You Swim in the Sea in Tenerife in Winter?
can-you-swim-in-the-sea-in-tenerife-in-w.meta: Yes. Sea temperatures sit around 19°C at their winter lowest, which most northern Europeans find swimmable. What matters more is which coast you pick.
can-you-swim-in-the-sea-in-tenerife-in-w.alt: Swimmers in the sea at Playa de las Vistas
can-you-swim-in-the-sea-in-tenerife-in-w.short: Yes, and plenty of people do. The sea around Tenerife drops to roughly 19°C at its coldest in late winter and reaches about 23°C in early autumn. Most northern Europeans find 19°C perfectly swimmable; if you are used to Mediterranean summers, it will feel brisk for the first minute.

p: The Atlantic here is remarkably stable. The coldest water comes in February, March and April, sitting somewhere around nineteen degrees, and the warmest in September and October at roughly twenty-three. That is a narrower swing than most of Europe manages, and it is why the island sells itself on year-round swimming rather than a summer season.

Nineteen degrees is colder than a heated pool and warmer than the sea off Britain, Ireland or Scandinavia in any month. Whether that reads as pleasant or bracing depends entirely on what you are used to. Children tend to mind it less than adults.

This matters more than the temperature. The sheltered southern beaches — Playa de las Vistas, Playa del Camisón, Playa del Duque, Fañabé — sit behind breakwaters that keep the water flat, and they are swimmable through the winter on most days.

The north and west are a different story in winter. Atlantic swell builds from roughly October through March, and beaches such as Playa Jardín, El Bollullo and the Anaga coast are frequently rough enough to be closed to swimming. This is the season when the seawater lidos at Lago Martiánez and the rock pools at Garachico and Punta del Hidalgo either come into their own or close entirely, depending on the day.

sections.h2: The pool question nobody asks in time
p: If you are travelling between November and March and a pool matters to you, check whether the hotel's pool is heated before you book, not after. Many southern hotels heat theirs through the winter and advertise it; plenty do not, and an unheated pool in January is noticeably colder than the sea.

The other winter reality is wind rather than water. The trade winds ease in winter compared with summer, which is good news for the beach, but the sun sits lower and drops sooner. Afternoons on the sand are shorter than the temperature suggests.
list: Around 19°C at the winter low, 23°C at the autumn high
Sheltered southern beaches swim through winter
North and west often too rough from October
Check whether the hotel pool is heated

faq: What is the sea temperature in Tenerife in December?
Around twenty degrees, easing towards nineteen through February and March. It is one of the warmest sea temperatures available in Europe in winter.
Is Tenerife warm enough to swim in January?
For most northern European visitors, yes, on the sheltered southern beaches. The water is cooler than in summer but the swing across the year is small.
Which beaches are best for winter swimming in Tenerife?
The breakwater-sheltered southern beaches: Playa de las Vistas, Playa del Camisón, Playa del Duque and Fañabé. Avoid the exposed north and west coasts, which are at their roughest in winter.
related: The calmest big beach in the south

is-tenerife-good-for-families.question: Is Tenerife good for families?
is-tenerife-good-for-families.title: Is Tenerife Good for Families? What to Know
is-tenerife-good-for-families.meta: Tenerife is one of Europe's strongest family destinations: calm sheltered beaches, two world-class attractions and reliable warmth in every month.
is-tenerife-good-for-families.alt: Sunbeds and swimmers at Playa de las Vistas
is-tenerife-good-for-families.short: Very. Short flights from most of Europe, no time difference from the UK and Portugal, warmth in every month, sheltered beaches where children can actually swim, and in Siam Park and Loro Parque two attractions good enough to build days around. The main decision is which resort, not whether.

p: The practical things first. Flights from northern Europe are four to five hours, there is no jet lag to speak of, and the climate means a February half-term feels like a summer holiday. Spain is comfortable with children in restaurants at hours that would raise eyebrows elsewhere, and highchairs, baby-changing and pharmacies are all easy to find.

Then the beaches. Playa de las Vistas and Playa del Camisón sit behind breakwaters that keep the water genuinely flat, and both have lifeguards in season. That is a meaningful difference from an open Atlantic beach, and it is why families cluster on this stretch of coast.

Siam Park above Costa Adeje is the strongest single attraction on the island and comfortably fills a day, with the Lost City area built for younger children and height restrictions on the bigger slides — worth checking before you promise anything. Loro Parque in the north pairs a large animal collection with a botanical garden, and a twin ticket covering both is sold at either park.

Beyond those, whale-watching trips from Los Cristianos and Puerto Colón have an unusually high success rate because the pilot whales here are resident rather than migratory, and the shorter two-hour trips suit younger children better than the full-day sails.
Costa Adeje is the safest choice: the best-maintained beaches, the strongest hotels and a flat seafront promenade you can walk with a pushchair. It is also the most expensive part of the island.

Los Cristianos costs less for the same sunshine and has an old town with a real centre, which some families prefer to a purpose-built resort. Playa de las Américas is cheaper again and has good beaches, but choose the hotel carefully — a block near the Veronicas nightlife strip is cheap for a reason, and the difference between a quiet street and a loud one can be two hundred metres.
The north is greener and considerably cheaper, at the cost of cooler, cloudier weather and rougher sea. It suits families who want to explore more than sunbathe.
list: Sheltered beaches with lifeguards in season
Siam Park and Loro Parque, plus a twin ticket
Four to five hours from northern Europe
Costa Adeje for ease, Los Cristianos for value

faq: Which part of Tenerife is best for families?
Costa Adeje for the best beaches and hotels, Los Cristianos for better value with a real town centre. Both have calm, lifeguarded beaches and flat seafront promenades.
Is Siam Park suitable for young children?
Yes. The Lost City area is built for them and there is a wave pool and a lazy river. Height restrictions apply on the bigger slides, so check them before the day.
Do you need a car in Tenerife with children?
Not if you are staying in the southern resorts, where the seafront is flat and walkable and buses cover the coast. A car helps if you plan to see Teide, Anaga or the north.
Is the sea warm enough for children?
It ranges from about 19°C in late winter to 23°C in early autumn. Children generally mind the cooler end less than adults do.

tenerife-or-lanzarote.question: Tenerife or Lanzarote — which should you choose?
tenerife-or-lanzarote.title: Tenerife or Lanzarote? An Honest Comparison
tenerife-or-lanzarote.meta: Lanzarote is starker, lower-rise and windier; Tenerife is bigger, greener in parts and has far more to do. Which suits which kind of trip.
tenerife-or-lanzarote.alt: A volcanic cone in the Timanfaya area of Lanzarote
tenerife-or-lanzarote.short: Choose Tenerife if you want variety — Teide, laurel forest, cities, nightlife and enough to fill two weeks. Choose Lanzarote if you want a stark volcanic landscape, César Manrique's architecture and a quieter, lower-rise island where nothing is more than an hour away.

p: Lanzarote looks like nowhere else in Europe. The eruptions of the 1730s buried a third of the island and left the Timanfaya badlands, a field of cinder cones and frozen lava that is still hot enough underground to be demonstrated to visitors. Vines grow in pits dug into black ash. It is austere, and people either love it immediately or find it bleak.

Tenerife is larger and far more varied. Teide rises to 3,715 metres, the Anaga range holds a subtropical laurel forest, and the north is green in a way Lanzarote never is. You can have a desert morning and a forest afternoon, which is not an option on the smaller island.

Tenerife wins on volume. Siam Park and Loro Parque are the best attractions in the archipelago, whale watching runs year-round off the south-west coast, and Santa Cruz and La Laguna give you proper cities with markets, tapas and a carnival second only to Rio. If rain or wind spoils a day, there is an alternative.

Lanzarote's draw is more curated. The island's identity was shaped by one man: the artist César Manrique, whose interventions — the Jameos del Agua caves, the Mirador del Río, the Cactus Garden — are genuinely worth the trip, and whose influence produced the building rules that keep the island low-rise and largely free of high-rise blocks. Playa Papagayo in the south is as good a beach as either island offers.

Both are warm year-round. Lanzarote is drier and noticeably windier, which suits watersports and suits sunbathing rather less — the beaches often have windbreaks for a reason. Tenerife's south is more sheltered; its north is cooler and cloudier than anywhere on Lanzarote.

Lanzarote is small enough to see properly in a week with a car, and nowhere is much more than an hour away. Tenerife is big enough that a week means choosing, and two weeks is not too many. If you want to lie still near one very good beach, Lanzarote makes it easy. If you want to keep moving, Tenerife gives you more to move towards.
list: Lanzarote: Timanfaya, Manrique, low-rise, windier
Tenerife: Teide, forests, cities, nightlife, more variety
Both warm all year; Lanzarote drier and breezier
Lanzarote fits a week; Tenerife rewards two

faq: Which is better for a first Canary Islands trip?
Tenerife, for most people — it has more variety and more to fall back on. Lanzarote is the better choice if the volcanic landscape and Manrique's work are what draw you.
Is Lanzarote windier than Tenerife?
Generally yes. Lanzarote is flatter and more exposed, and beach windbreaks are common. Tenerife's south-west coast is more sheltered.
Which has better beaches?

Lanzarote's Papagayo beaches are outstanding and largely undeveloped. Tenerife has more beaches overall and more serviced ones, with imported golden sand in the south and black volcanic sand elsewhere.

can-you-get-to-teide-by-bus.question: Can you get to Mount Teide by bus?
can-you-get-to-teide-by-bus.title: Can You Get to Mount Teide by Bus?
can-you-get-to-teide-by-bus.meta: Yes. Two TITSA buses reach Teide National Park daily, one from Costa Adeje and one from Puerto de la Cruz. What they give you, and what they do not.
can-you-get-to-teide-by-bus.alt: The Teide cable car with snow on the crater floor
can-you-get-to-teide-by-bus.short: Yes. TITSA line 342 runs up from Costa Adeje and line 348 from Puerto de la Cruz, each once a day — up in the morning, back in the afternoon. It works, and it is cheap, but it fixes your day to a single window of roughly four hours in the park.

sections.h2: The two services, and what they actually give you
p: Line 342 climbs from Costa Adeje, picking up along the southern resorts, and line 348 comes up from Puerto de la Cruz on the north side. Both run once each way per day: up in the morning, back in the early to mid afternoon. Between them they cover the main stops on the crater floor, including the cable car base station and the Roques de García.

That single daily return is the whole catch. You get roughly four hours in the park, and you cannot extend it — miss the bus down and there is no later one. It is enough for the cable car and a short walk, or for the Roques de García loop and lunch, but not comfortably for both.

sections.h2: What the bus does not include
p: The bus takes you to the park, not up the mountain. The cable car is a separate ticket and should be booked online in advance, particularly in peak season, because walk-up availability is unreliable and you cannot afford to queue when your ride home leaves at a fixed time.

Going above the cable car's top station to the actual crater rim needs a free permit, booked separately through the national parks reservation site, and the daily quota goes early. If that is your plan, the bus is a tight way to do it — a hire car or a tour gives you the slack you will want.
Check the current timetable before you commit. TITSA adjusts these services seasonally, and an out-of-date departure time is the single most common way this trip goes wrong.
list: One return service per day on each line
Roughly four hours in the park
Cable car ticket booked separately
Summit permit is free but must be pre-booked

sections.h2: When a tour or a car makes more sense
p: If you want the sunset above the clouds, or the stargazing, the bus cannot help you — it is long gone. Organised tours from the southern resorts cover exactly that gap, and the sunset-and-stars trips are the reason most people book one.

A hire car gives you the most freedom and costs the least per head if there are three or four of you, at the price of driving mountain roads. The TF-21 from Vilaflor and the TF-38 are well surfaced but continuously winding, and it is a long climb. Whatever you arrive in, dress for below freezing: the crater floor sits above two thousand metres and behaves nothing like the coast.

faq: How much does the bus to Teide cost?
A few euros each way on TITSA, which makes it by far the cheapest way up. Check current fares, and consider a ten-trip card if you will use the buses elsewhere.
How long do you get at Teide with the bus?
Roughly four hours, fixed by the single daily return. Enough for the cable car or the Roques de García, but tight for both.
Can you do Teide sunset or stargazing by bus?
No. The buses return in the afternoon. Evening trips need a hire car or an organised tour.
Do the buses go to the top of Teide?
No. They stop on the crater floor, including at the cable car base station. The cable car takes you higher, and the final path to the summit needs a separate free permit.

do-you-tip-in-tenerife.question: Do you tip in Tenerife?
do-you-tip-in-tenerife.title: Do You Tip in Tenerife? What's Normal
do-you-tip-in-tenerife.meta: Tipping is not obligatory in Tenerife and service is included in the price. Rounding up or leaving 5–10% for good service is generous, not expected.
do-you-tip-in-tenerife.alt: A seafood rice dish with langoustine
do-you-tip-in-tenerife.short: Not obligatory, and nobody will chase you. Spanish menu prices include tax and service, so a tip is a genuine extra rather than a top-up of someone's wage. Rounding up the bill, or leaving five to ten per cent after a good meal, is generous by local standards.

p: Considerably less than visitors assume. In an everyday bar or café, Canarians typically leave the small change from the bill and nothing more. After a proper restaurant meal they might round up to the nearest note, or leave a few euros on a larger table if the service was good.

The reason is structural rather than mean-spirited. Spanish hospitality staff are paid a wage rather than a tipped minimum, and the price on the menu is the price you pay, tax and service included. Nobody's income depends on your arithmetic, which takes the anxiety out of the whole thing.

It is worth unlearning American habits here in particular. A twenty per cent tip is not generous in Tenerife so much as conspicuous, and staff in the resort areas have simply learned that some visitors do it. Nobody is offended, but nobody is expecting it either.

Restaurants: round up, or five to ten per cent for service you actually noticed. Ten is at the generous end. Bars and cafés: leave the coins. Taxis: round up to the next euro or two — meters are used and the fare is the fare.

Hotels: entirely optional. A euro or two for a porter, or a few left for housekeeping at the end of a stay, is a kind gesture rather than an expectation. Boat crews and walking guides: a few euros each if you enjoyed the trip, and they will not be surprised either way.
rows: round up to the next euro
Meters are used; the fare is the fare
a few euros at the end

p: Check the bill before adding anything. A minority of restaurants in the busiest tourist streets add a service charge, and if servicio is already on there, adding ten per cent on top is simply paying twice. It is not a scam, just something to read.

The other is newer: card machines in tourist areas that present a screen of pre-set tip percentages before you pay. That prompt is an imported habit, not a Canarian one, and there is no awkwardness in choosing the no-tip option or handing over cash instead. Tipping here is a thank-you, not a tax.
list: Service and tax are already in the price
Read the bill for servicio before adding more
Card-machine tip prompts are an import, not a custom
Cash is easier for the person actually serving you

faq: Is it rude not to tip in Tenerife?
No. Leaving nothing in a bar is completely normal, and in a restaurant nobody will comment. Tipping is appreciated rather than expected.
How much do you tip a taxi driver in Tenerife?
Rounding up to the next euro or two is plenty. Taxis are metered and there is no expectation beyond that.
Do you tip in all-inclusive hotels in Tenerife?
Not required. Some guests leave a few euros for bar or restaurant staff they see repeatedly, or for housekeeping at the end of the stay. It is a gesture, not an obligation.
Should I tip in cash or on the card?
Cash, if you can. It reaches the person who served you more reliably than a figure added to a card payment.

day-trip-to-la-gomera-from-tenerife.question: Can you do a day trip to La Gomera from Tenerife?
day-trip-to-la-gomera-from-tenerife.title: Day Trip to La Gomera from Tenerife: How It Works
day-trip-to-la-gomera-from-tenerife.meta: Yes — ferries from Los Cristianos reach San Sebastián de la Gomera in under an hour. What you can realistically see in a day, and the hire-car trap.
day-trip-to-la-gomera-from-tenerife.alt: San Sebastián de la Gomera above the Atlantic, with Tenerife on the horizon
day-trip-to-la-gomera-from-tenerife.short: Yes. Fast ferries from Los Cristianos reach San Sebastián de la Gomera in under an hour, several times a day, which makes a day trip entirely practical. It is a long day and you will only scratch the island — but the ferry is the easy part, and getting around once you land is what needs planning.

sections.h2: Getting there is the simple bit
p: Ferries leave from the harbour at Los Cristianos, which is also where the whale-watching boats go from. The fast catamaran crossing to San Sebastián takes under an hour, and there are several departures a day in each direction, so an early boat out and a late one back is a realistic plan.

More than one operator runs the route, at different speeds and prices. Book ahead in peak season and at weekends, and give yourself a margin at the Tenerife end — the harbour car park fills and the check-in cut-off is real.

This catches people out every year, so it is worth stating plainly: most Tenerife hire-car agreements do not permit taking the vehicle to another island. Turning up at the ferry with a rental car and no permission can void your insurance entirely. Read your contract, and if you want a car on La Gomera, either clear it with the company in advance or book one to collect in San Sebastián.

The alternative is an organised excursion sold from the southern resorts, which bundles the ferry with a coach tour and removes the problem. For a first visit that is the low-friction option. Public buses on La Gomera exist but are infrequent and will not get you around the island in a day.

San Sebastián itself is a pleasant hour or two: a small harbour town where Columbus took on water before crossing the Atlantic in 1492, a fact the town has not forgotten. Beyond it, the island climbs fast and the roads are slow and continuously winding — distances that look short on a map take much longer than you expect.

The single thing most worth the drive is Garajonay National Park, a UNESCO-listed laurel forest that survives from a time when this vegetation covered much of southern Europe. It is misty, ancient and completely unlike anywhere in Tenerife's south. Valle Gran Rey on the west coast is the other classic, though it is a long way for a day trip. You may also come across a demonstration of silbo, the whistled form of Spanish used to talk across the island's ravines and recognised by UNESCO.
Honest verdict: one day gives you a taste and a long ferry day. La Gomera rewards an overnight far more than it rewards a dash.
list: Under an hour by fast ferry from Los Cristianos
Garajonay laurel forest is the highlight
Check your hire-car contract before boarding
An overnight beats a day trip if you can

faq: How long is the ferry from Tenerife to La Gomera?
Under an hour on the fast catamaran from Los Cristianos to San Sebastián. Slower services take longer and usually cost less.
Can you take a hire car from Tenerife to La Gomera?
Usually not. Most Tenerife rental agreements forbid inter-island travel and doing it anyway can void your insurance. Check your contract, or hire a car on La Gomera instead.
Is a day trip to La Gomera worth it?
Yes if you accept it is a taste rather than a tour. Garajonay National Park is the reason to go. If you can spare a night, the island is far better over two days.
What is silbo?
Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish developed to carry across La Gomera's deep ravines. It is recognised by UNESCO and taught in the island's schools.

tenerife-south-or-north-airport.question: Should you fly into Tenerife South or Tenerife North?
tenerife-south-or-north-airport.title: Tenerife South or North Airport? Which to Choose
tenerife-south-or-north-airport.meta: Tenerife South (TFS) serves the southern resorts; Tenerife North (TFN) suits Puerto de la Cruz, La Laguna and Santa Cruz. Pick by where you are staying.
tenerife-south-or-north-airport.alt: The west coast of Tenerife from the air
tenerife-south-or-north-airport.short: Pick by where you are staying, not by fare alone. Tenerife South (TFS) is about twenty minutes from Los Cristianos and Costa Adeje and takes most international flights. Tenerife North (TFN) suits Puerto de la Cruz, Santa Cruz and the north, but is over an hour from the southern resorts.

p: This is the one most visitors use. It sits on the south-east coast near El Médano and handles the great majority of international and charter traffic, which is why the cheap package flights land here.

From arrivals it is roughly fifteen to twenty minutes to Los Cristianos and Playa de las Américas, and twenty to twenty-five to Costa Adeje. Taxis, pre-booked transfers, hire cars and TITSA buses all serve it, and if you are staying anywhere on the southern strip this is simply the right airport.

The northern airport sits just above La Laguna, about fifteen minutes from there and from Santa Cruz, and thirty to forty from Puerto de la Cruz. It handles most inter-island flights and a lot of mainland Spanish traffic, plus a smaller number of international routes.

One practical quirk: it sits at around 630 metres, high enough that low cloud rolls across it when the coast below is clear. Flights operate through it routinely, but if you land in mist having left sunshine in the south, that is why.
The trap is distance. TFN to Costa Adeje is well over an hour by road, and a transfer priced on that distance can wipe out whatever you saved on the fare.

sections.h2: How to choose in one line
p: Staying anywhere from Los Cristianos to Los Gigantes, fly into South. Staying in Puerto de la Cruz, La Orotava, La Laguna or Santa Cruz, fly into North if the schedule allows. Touring the whole island with a hire car, either works — pick on price and timing.

Two footnotes. If you are island-hopping, inter-island flights mostly use the north, so a trip combining Tenerife with La Palma or El Hierro may want TFN at one end. And if you are arriving late at night, the shorter transfer is worth more than it looks on paper — an extra hour in a minibus after a delayed flight is nobody's idea of a holiday.
list: Southern resorts → Tenerife South (TFS)
Puerto de la Cruz, La Laguna, Santa Cruz → North (TFN)
TFN is 1h+ from the southern resorts
Inter-island flights mostly use TFN

faq: How far is Tenerife South Airport from Costa Adeje?
Roughly twenty to twenty-five minutes by road on the TF-1, and about fifteen to twenty to Los Cristianos.
Can you get from Tenerife North to the southern resorts?
Yes, but allow well over an hour by road. Bus, taxi, transfer and hire car are all available; the cost of the longer transfer often cancels out a cheaper flight.
Which airport is better for Puerto de la Cruz?
Tenerife North, at thirty to forty minutes, against roughly an hour and a quarter from the south.
Why is Tenerife North often cloudy?
It sits at around 630 metres on the north side, where trade-wind cloud banks up against the hills. The coast below can be clear while the airport is in mist.
